title: Ohio wants a seat for consumer advocates
speaker: Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel
text: Ohio’s consumer advocate asked FERC to give state consumer offices the same confidential access available to commissions. Customers need an advocate who can test costs and curtailment decisions, it argued. Its November 9 request challenges the October order. It does not ask PJM to publish customer records.

title: Who can see the customer-level data?
speaker: Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel
text: OCC sought rehearing of the October 9 order. It asked FERC to reject the registry unless PJM grants consumer advocates access under confidentiality agreements.

title: Aggregate figures or individual projects?
speaker: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (New Jersey)
text: Pallone wanted as much of the registry made public as possible to improve demand forecasts. FERC records his request separately from the states’ requests for protected access. He spoke as a member of Congress.

title: Pennsylvania asks to see curtailment data
speaker: Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission
text: Pennsylvania’s commission supported creating a registry but wanted state commissions to have access and wanted PJM to record curtailments. Its comments addressed the proposal before FERC rejected interim curtailment service.
locator: PDF p. 8, section II, Large Load Registry

title: States need usable records to set retail rules
speaker: Organization of PJM States
text: OPSI wanted meaningful state access to the registry to set retail curtailment rules and allocate costs. Its September comments distinguish the registry, which it supported, from the compensation mechanism it challenged.

title: Give customers a chance to correct errors
speaker: Equinix and PJM industrial customers
text: Equinix wanted customers notified and allowed to verify or correct the information PJM would use. Industrial customers also requested an appeal and safeguards for commercial data.

title: Who answers for a supplier’s data?
speaker: Southern Maryland Electric Cooperative
text: The cooperative asked who bears liability when a distributor reports information obtained from another party, how it could recover its compliance costs, and whether the reporting manual would be filed for review.

title: A registry cannot tell an operator what just tripped
speaker: Independent Market Monitor for PJM
text: The market monitor distinguished enrollment data from real-time telemetry. It said PJM had not shown how it would measure an actual reduction in the proposed interim service.

title: Which customers should lose power first?
speaker: Commissioner David Rosner
text: Rosner wanted voluntary demand response called first, followed by noncritical large loads before homes and other ordinary customers. He objected to keeping demand out of the capacity market forecast. His October concurrence predates the November compliance filing.

title: Existing generators may gain from the rejection
speaker: Jefferies analysts, quoted by Utility Dive
text: Jefferies saw the rejection of interim service as favorable to existing independent generators. That was an analyst assessment of market effects, separate from the commission’s reasons for its decision.

title: A longer wait for private deals
speaker: Mary Yang, 804 Advisory, interviewed by Latitude Media
text: Yang, a former PJM regulatory counsel, expected other priorities to delay a rewrite. She said that uncertainty could slow bilateral arrangements between new loads and generators.
locator: Maeve Allsup, October 13, interview with Mary Yang

title: Swett wanted a record FERC could test
speaker: Chairman Laura Swett
text: Swett said the original procurement arrived too late for a deficiency letter or further evidence. She urged a prompt section 205 filing to repair the rejected terms. Her September concurrence did not address the later timetable.

title: Rosner would charge zones with data center growth
speaker: Commissioner David Rosner
text: Rosner supported directing costs to zones whose data center growth drove the shortfall. He called on states to set retail tariffs, enforce collateral and decide curtailment priorities. He wanted a return to ordinary hedging and capacity procurement after the backstop.

title: See wanted the forecast tied to the bill
speaker: Commissioner Lindsay See
text: See wanted dependable generation quickly but said the first proposal left existing customers exposed. Better evidence about which projects will actually connect should guide who pays for the resulting capacity.

title: LaCerte tied speed to ratepayer protection
speaker: Commissioner David LaCerte
text: LaCerte urged PJM to refile promptly rather than wait for more briefs. He said new loads should pay for the capacity they require and cited the commitment to build, bring or buy that capacity.

title: A promise to pay is only as good as its security
speaker: Commissioner Judy Chang
text: In the separate Duke case, Chang dissented because Duke had not shown that its security requirements backed the full 15-year payment promise. The comparison bears on PJM’s proposed collateral; Chang was not evaluating PJM’s dollar amount.
locator: Chang dissent, section on security requirements

title: Ohio wants charges to reach the customers responsible
speaker: Office of the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel
text: On rehearing of the September order, OCC argued that households should not pay to cover a shortfall caused by data centers. It separately questioned FERC’s decision to allow sellers to receive their own bid prices.

title: Consumer advocates question a 15-year commitment
speaker: Joint Consumer Advocates, including Delaware, D.C., Illinois, Maryland and New Jersey offices
text: The advocates estimated that buying 15 years rather than five could add $13 billion. They also warned that without a location requirement, customers could pay for capacity built far from the shortfall. These were their estimates and objections to the September order.

title: West Virginia warns restrictive offsets could drive an overbuy
speaker: Public Service Commission of West Virginia
text: The West Virginia commission warned that complex rules could discourage participants from reporting qualifying capacity. That would make the final purchase larger than necessary.
locator: PDF pp. 2–4, bilateral matching and offsets

title: Update the need when a project drops out
speaker: Organization of PJM States
text: OPSI asked PJM to remove withdrawn large projects when setting the procurement target. Otherwise existing customers could pay for generation to meet demand that no longer exists.

title: New Jersey wanted demand-side bids to have room to compete
speaker: New Jersey Board of Public Utilities
text: The New Jersey board sought more flexible terms for demand resources and distributed resource aggregations in the original procurement. This concerned auction eligibility; it did not endorse the later peak-shaving formula.

title: Fifteen years of bills on one forecast
speaker: Illinois Commerce Commission and Joint Consumer Advocates
text: Illinois regulators and the consumer advocates warned that a single end date for contracts could amplify forecast errors. FERC recorded that concern as it considered freezing load shares at one point in time.

title: AMP distinguishes local load from regional growth
speaker: American Municipal Power
text: AMP asked FERC to protect systems that did not cause the new demand. It also disputed the suggestion that the forecast table excluded projects PJM had actually counted.

title: The transmission owners dispute who can impose an exit charge
speaker: Indicated PJM Transmission Owners
text: The owners argued that FERC should reject the original exit amendment on cost-causation grounds and that their agreement reserved the relevant filing right to them. Their rehearing request concerned the earlier wording.

title: Constellation asks who benefits when an owner leaves
speaker: Constellation Energy Generation
text: Constellation asked FERC to clarify that it had not assigned the departing owner’s share to suppliers by default. In its view an exiting owner, rather than captive customers, should bear exit costs it causes.

title: FirstEnergy challenged the earlier security requirement
speaker: FirstEnergy Service Company
text: FirstEnergy compared supplier security of $1.5 million per MW under the earlier design with the much smaller security required of sellers. That objection is a benchmark for the revised calculation, not an objection to the new $686,000 figure.

title: Who pays after a generator starts operating?
speaker: FirstEnergy Service Company
text: FirstEnergy said the original shortfall charge stopped once a generator reached commercial operation. It questioned whether a seller then had sufficient incentive to perform throughout its 15-year term.

title: Should the original forecast bind even if load never arrives?
speaker: Amazon and Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative
text: Amazon argued that immutable shares would diverge from actual demand as projects changed. NOVEC asked why PJM considered a single snapshot appropriate.

title: DOE wanted individual loads identified before allocation
speaker: U.S. Department of Energy
text: DOE wanted a mandatory way to identify the large load driving additional procurement and give it a chance to build, bring or buy capacity. It questioned whether the proposed two-year lookback would capture the relevant projects.

title: The market monitor wanted new physical supply
speaker: Independent Market Monitor for PJM
text: The monitor objected to eligibility rules that could let an existing resource reclassify its capacity. Its test was whether an award actually paid for additional physical supply.

title: NOVEC disputes attributing the whole shortage to large loads
speaker: Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative
text: NOVEC identified causes of the capacity shortage besides growth in large loads. It preferred voluntary subscription, with interruptible service for a customer that declined. It is a cooperative, not the Virginia regulator.

title: Two state commissions back the parallel study
speaker: Mississippi and Louisiana Public Service Commissions
text: The commissions backed a 120-day joint study. They said studying the load and its generator together could avoid duplicating network upgrades; the limit of ten pairs per period made it manageable. They wanted a permanent process so projects could plan and finance construction.

title: Arkansas signs on to the Southern regulators’ case
speaker: Arkansas Public Service Commission
text: Arkansas expressly agreed with the Mississippi and Louisiana commissions’ comments and asked FERC to accept MISO’s tariff changes. It did not offer its own numerical estimate of costs or queue delays.
locator: Comments of the Arkansas PSC, concluding paragraph (unpaginated)

title: Consumer offices question the treatment of existing load
speaker: Iowa Office of Consumer Advocate, Illinois and Michigan attorneys general, Minnesota Department of Commerce and co-protesters
text: The joint protesters asked how the study would prevent costs shifting to other customers. They warned that related MISO proposals could exempt about 30 GW of existing load from some reliability requirements; 30 GW was not the size of the proposed LARS study queue.

title: Google backs co-study but wants safeguards for independent bids
speaker: Google
text: Google supported studying loads and generators together but questioned the separate assumptions used in the ordinary queue. It wanted cost protections and a way for independent generators to participate without discrimination by the serving utility.

title: Bloom proposes 50 MW without delaying the filing
speaker: Bloom Energy
text: Bloom backed the study but challenged its 200 MW entry threshold. It proposed letting transmission-connected loads of at least 50 MW participate and asked FERC not to delay the requested start date.

title: Who gets first claim on spare grid capacity?
speaker: American Clean Power Association and Southern Renewable Energy Association
text: The trade associations said studying accelerated projects without other generators already waiting could leave later studies with fewer feasible connections and higher costs. They objected to a permanent parallel route without a cap on total capacity.

title: Solar developers challenge a utility veto
speaker: Solar Energy Industries Association and Advanced Energy United
text: The protesters asked FERC to reject the proposal or clarify that an applicant meeting all published requirements could not lose access at the transmission customer’s discretion.

title: A parallel queue can promise the same grid capacity twice
speaker: Clean Energy Advocates
text: The advocates warned that two study tracks using different assumptions could count the same unused transmission capacity twice. They challenged assigning upgrade costs to existing customers based on agreements whose terms FERC had not seen.

title: Utilities say deposits and commitments screen speculative requests
speaker: Alliant Energy and Consumers Energy
text: The utilities backed the readiness requirements because a speculative project could occupy one of a limited number of study slots. They argued the joint model could identify cheaper combined upgrades.

title: Entergy and Cleco contrast 120 days with years in the regular queue
speaker: Entergy and Cleco
text: The utilities said some ordinary MISO study cycles had taken four years or more. They supported the 120-day path and argued that its cap of ten load-generator pairs per study period would keep it workable.

title: DTE sees a binding match as evidence of readiness
speaker: DTE Electric
text: DTE supported the pairing rules and minimum commitment as evidence of a lasting commercial relationship. It also said the tariff allowed the interconnection customer to participate even though the transmission customer submits the application.

title: State organization asks for protection of existing queue positions
speaker: Organization of MISO States, quoted by Utility Dive
text: OMS warned that a rapid route must not turn into a general substitute for the queue. It asked for safeguards before qualifying pairs could claim transmission capacity ahead of projects already waiting.
locator: October 26, reporting on October 23 ER27-25 comments

title: Chang dissented over the lack of dedicated security
speaker: Commissioner Judy Chang
text: Chang said Duke had not demonstrated that a promise to pay for 75% of forecast demand would protect existing customers if the responsible utility defaulted. She wanted security commensurate with the 15-year commitment.
locator: Chang dissent, section on security requirements (unpaginated DOCX)

title: See accepts 75% but calls it a low-end safeguard
speaker: Commissioner Lindsay See
text: See saw the minimum revenue commitment as an improvement over charging for use alone. She said 75% might be near the low end of an acceptable range and urged Duke to consider incremental charges where appropriate.
locator: See concurrence, discussion of committed revenue contribution (unpaginated DOCX)

title: Rosner calls the tariff an improvement, with risk left over
speaker: Commissioner David Rosner
text: Rosner said Duke’s previous tariff contained no comparable protection for households or small businesses. He accepted the added protection and said FERC should consider more if action by the states proved insufficient.
locator: Rosner concurrence, first and second points (unpaginated DOCX)

title: States object to members controlling access to FERC
speaker: OPSI and PJM Governors’ Collaborative governance negotiating team
text: Before the vote, the states’ negotiating team opposed the members’ term sheet. The team said the proposed supermajority requirement would let private members decide whether a state proposal received equal consideration at FERC. It preferred a direct route for states to be heard.

title: LaCerte points to gridlock in PJM’s stakeholder process
speaker: Commissioner David LaCerte
text: At WIRES on July 9, LaCerte said PJM’s stakeholder process too often protected individual business interests and prevented agreement. He was discussing governance months before the members voted, not evaluating their final term sheet.

title: How does a new load forecast change the capacity purchase?
speaker: Chairman Laura Swett
text: Swett asked the October reliability panel how to model the scale and operating patterns of large loads. She pointed out that the forecast determines how much generation is procured and therefore influences market prices.

title: Chang questions the incentive to stay flexible after connection
speaker: Commissioner Judy Chang
text: Chang asked why a data center would voluntarily disconnect once connected if each interrupted megawatt-hour was very costly. She invited utilities and operators to explain what would make a flexibility commitment credible.

title: Who pays when a data center brings its own generator?
speaker: Commissioner David LaCerte
text: Answering Senator Cotton, LaCerte said beneficiaries should pay for the new infrastructure and states should hold hyperscalers to their commitments in retail rates. He did not specify a PJM cost formula.

title: MISO proposes parallel studies for paired load and generation
speaker: Midcontinent Independent System Operator
text: MISO proposed LARS in a separate section 205 docket. It argued that modeling a matched pair could identify upgrades for the combination instead of each project separately. This was one proposed response to the June concerns, not a final decision on the full show cause case.

title: Tribal transmission owner says it has no end-use customers
speaker: Morongo Transmission LLC
text: Morongo said it leases transmission capacity and receives revenue through CAISO’s access charge. Because it serves no end-use customers, it argued that its own tariff needed no amendment. It still intended to participate in the proceeding.

title: CAISO describes the board’s plan before filing
speaker: Elliot Mainzer, CAISO president and CEO, quoted by APPA
text: After the October board action, Mainzer said CAISO expected its response to improve operational visibility, protect other customers from cost shifts and speed connections for flexible loads. His statement described a plan, not FERC approval.

title: AMP wanted an enforceable route back to the show cause case
speaker: American Municipal Power
text: AMP opposed an unconditional delay and asked FERC to require a compliance filing. The order says FERC would return to the section 206 case for any preliminary finding MISO’s tariff filings did not address.
locator: Discussion of AMP’s protest and Commission determination (unpaginated)

title: Why SPP asked for five more days than other operators
speaker: Southwest Power Pool
text: SPP told FERC its board meeting had moved because of the elections. The revised November 17 vote made a November 16 filing impractical; FERC granted a November 20 response date.

title: Six municipal owners and WAPA distinguished themselves from investor-owned utilities
speaker: Six Cities and Western Area Power Administration
text: These public owners committed to coordinate with CAISO and file changes if necessary. FERC rescinded the show cause order as to them; the other California respondents remained in the case.
locator: Commission determination on Six Cities and WAPA (unpaginated)

title: Constellation challenges the July 2028 date
speaker: Constellation and PJM
text: Constellation questioned the proposed July 2028 start for interim network service. PJM answered that administering interruptions required new automation, but said it expected to take requests from September 2027.

title: AMP identifies a missing class of behind-the-meter generation
speaker: American Municipal Power and PJM
text: AMP asked that the new service also cover non-retail behind-the-meter generation. PJM agreed to revise the language. On a separate objection from Amtrak and industrial customers, PJM said its changes did not impose the netting restriction they feared.

title: Which part could be filed in August?
speaker: PJM and Constellation
text: PJM sought an extension to align its co-location and large-load work. Constellation wanted full interim network-service terms on the original schedule. FERC kept the August partial filing while granting additional time for other requirements.
locator: Requests and ruling on extension of time (unpaginated)

title: Pennsylvania’s consumer advocate challenges regional cost sharing
speaker: Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate
text: The office asked FERC to clarify that a customer agreement is only one protection. It wanted parties to be able to show that existing regional allocation methods themselves charge other customers for network upgrades needed by a large load.

title: Four state offices want the full upgrade cost charged to the new load
speaker: Maryland Office of People’s Counsel, Ohio Consumers’ Counsel, Delaware Division of the Public Advocate and Illinois Attorney General
text: The four offices backed FERC’s transparency directives but said disclosure alone leaves existing cost shifts intact. They asked that agreements require full payment for the necessary upgrades and that other customers receive the corresponding revenue credits promptly.

title: An Indiana representative asks for federal review of large-load projects
speaker: Rep. Victoria Spartz (Indiana’s 5th Congressional District)
text: Spartz asked FERC and DOE to scrutinize potentially duplicate load forecasts and to require developers to pay attributable generation and transmission costs. Her November letter represents a member of Congress, not Indiana’s utility commission.

title: What MISO’s regional report leaves out
speaker: Organization of MISO States
text: OMS said the report does not fully reflect state proceedings on resource planning, retail rates and utility approvals because MISO is not a party to those proceedings. It wanted regional planning to complement, rather than displace, state responsibility for adequacy.

title: Missouri supports five extra days to secure a state review
speaker: Missouri Public Service Commission
text: Missouri backed the 95-day request because SPP’s November 17 board vote fell just beyond the 90-day window. It said the extra days allowed meaningful state input without materially delaying the case.

title: SPP’s state committee wanted time to develop a cost proposal
speaker: SPP Regional State Committee
text: The committee endorsed a November 20 deadline while its cost-allocation team studied who should secure network costs if promised demand fails to arrive or leaves early. The filing endorsed the schedule, not a final cost-allocation formula.

title: New England states back time for regional deliberation
speaker: New England States Committee on Electricity
text: NESCOE, the committee representing the six New England states, supported the requested delay. It wanted the states and stakeholders to be able to examine proposed tariff changes through the region’s existing process.

title: Support for more time came with a reservation
speaker: Organization of MISO States
text: OMS supported time for a coordinated sequence of filings but said granting abeyance should neither narrow the inquiry nor prejudge that the coming tariff changes would settle every issue.

title: Corporate buyers wanted time to test the California proposal
speaker: Corporate Energy Buyers Association
text: CEBA backed the California parties’ requests for 90 more days. It argued that testing proposals with stakeholders before filing could improve their commercial viability and legal durability.

title: Constellation supported more time with a condition
speaker: Constellation Energy Generation
text: Constellation supported a partial delay but said PJM’s separate duty to comply with the co-location order could not depend on the outcome of the large-load process.

title: Data center operators want the binding standard in the tariff
speaker: Data Center Coalition
text: The coalition asked FERC to reject the reliability proposal without prejudice and require substantive standards in the tariff itself. It said future changes should be filed with FERC rather than made outside the tariff.

title: Municipal utilities seek a clear limit on regulated loads
speaker: Midwest Transmission Dependent Utilities
text: The utilities said MISO’s answer disclaimed applying the rules to distribution-connected loads but the tariff still did not say so unambiguously. They wanted the tariff to explain how a utility could assign a compliance task to the large load.

title: MISO says independent generators can negotiate before applying
speaker: Midcontinent Independent System Operator
text: MISO said the transmission customer submits an application for an already matched pair. It argued that an independent generator remains free to bring a proposal to that customer before the application, and that the eligibility rules are nondiscretionary.

title: MISO defends a higher entry threshold
speaker: Midcontinent Independent System Operator
text: MISO defended 200 MW based on its experience with large-load studies. It said modeling the load and several associated plants together offered the largest potential savings where loads and upgrades were especially large.

title: MISO would proceed before the rest of the cost protections are approved
speaker: Midcontinent Independent System Operator
text: MISO said the study should go ahead before related cost-recovery reforms were complete. It promised to incorporate those protections once FERC accepted them and cited other existing tariff mechanisms.

title: Eolian wants nearby generation considered for permanent service
speaker: Eolian
text: Eolian sought clarification that generation located electrically close to a large load could qualify for permanent limited service if it could constrain grid withdrawals over the long term. FERC dismissed the request because the preliminary order was not final.

title: Eolian wants nearby generation considered for permanent service
speaker: Eolian
text: Eolian sought clarification that generation located electrically close to a large load could qualify for permanent limited service if it could constrain grid withdrawals over the long term. FERC dismissed the request because the preliminary order was not final.

title: Eolian wants nearby generation considered for permanent service
speaker: Eolian
text: Eolian sought clarification that generation located electrically close to a large load could qualify for permanent limited service if it could constrain grid withdrawals over the long term. FERC dismissed the request because the preliminary order was not final.

title: Eolian wants nearby generation considered for permanent service
speaker: Eolian
text: Eolian sought clarification that generation located electrically close to a large load could qualify for permanent limited service if it could constrain grid withdrawals over the long term. FERC dismissed the request because the preliminary order was not final.

title: See wants states to retain authority over retail service
speaker: Commissioner Lindsay See
text: See said the federal changes should give states better information about wholesale costs so they could carry out their own affordability duties. She cautioned against using federal tariff reform to override state decisions.

title: Chang asks for evidence before narrowing the states’ role
speaker: Commissioner Judy Chang
text: Chang supported developing a regional record. She welcomed evidence from state regulators on possible jurisdictional problems and distinguished the narrower preliminary findings from the broader federal authority contemplated in the national rulemaking.

title: LaCerte urged timely regional answers
speaker: Commissioner David LaCerte
text: LaCerte supported the order as a way to identify gaps in large-load tariffs. He expected a timely response with evidence about the region’s own rules, not a final nationwide tariff imposed in June.

title: Rosner wants commitments that survive a canceled project
speaker: Commissioner David Rosner
text: Rosner argued that a cost recovery agreement should prevent households from paying for a network upgrade if the data center never opens. He invited alternative regional mechanisms if they offered comparable protection.

title: Aggregate figures or individual projects?
speaker: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (New Jersey)
text: Pallone wanted as much of the registry made public as possible to improve demand forecasts. FERC records his request separately from the states’ requests for protected access. He spoke as a member of Congress.

title: Pennsylvania asks to see curtailment data
speaker: Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission
text: Pennsylvania’s commission supported creating a registry but wanted state commissions to have access and wanted PJM to record curtailments. Its comments addressed the proposal before FERC rejected interim curtailment service.
locator: PDF p. 8, section II, Large Load Registry

text: Equinix wanted customers notified and allowed to verify or correct the information PJM would use. Industrial customers also requested an appeal and safeguards for commercial data.

title: Chang explains why the June record needs upgrade costs
speaker: Commissioner Judy Chang
text: Answering Senator Hirono, Chang linked the June section 206 proceedings to tracking which data center triggered a network upgrade and identifying who would otherwise pay. She described the information needed to limit cost shifting, not the outcome of a regional case.

title: Rosner links investment signals to state confidence
speaker: Commissioner David Rosner
text: At the July hearing Rosner told Senator McCormick that market rules can send investment signals, but those signals lose force if states do not trust how prices are set. He wanted states involved in regional planning.

title: When is an interruption a substitute for capacity?
speaker: Commissioner David Rosner
text: PJM’s July report considered shortage service. Reviewing a subsequent tariff proposal in October, Rosner objected to mandatory curtailment before paid, voluntary demand response and warned about masking demand in capacity prices.

title: How California described its board-approved plan three months later
speaker: Elliot Mainzer, CAISO president and CEO, quoted by APPA
text: The July report scheduled a response for the fall. After the October board action, Mainzer said CAISO expected the proposed rules to improve operational awareness and reduce cost shifts. The board action did not itself change a FERC tariff.

title: State regulators raised the risk that a large project leaves early
speaker: SPP Regional State Committee
text: In its later comments on the filing schedule, the committee said its cost team was examining security for upgrades if a large customer never arrives or leaves early. It did not approve a particular conditional-service charge.
match: Conditional service has an end date

title: Exelon points to New England as a precedent for buying closer to delivery
speaker: Exelon Corporation
text: In a separate complaint about PJM, Exelon argued that moving procurement closer to delivery could reduce forecast risk. It invoked ISO New England as a precedent. The complaint sought changes in PJM, not changes to ISO New England’s July report.

title: Who decides if a regulated generation solution will go forward?
speaker: New York Independent System Operator
text: NYISO explained that if the market and transmission proposals cannot cover a reliability need, it may refer a non-transmission solution to the New York Public Service Commission. The state commission then considers the project and cost recovery. This is NYISO’s description of the process, not a state endorsement of a project.

title: SPP acknowledges an omitted West Region rate-sheet item
speaker: Southwest Power Pool
text: SPP’s November 10 amendment says the November 6 filing inadvertently omitted Schedule 14 and Incremental Market Efficiency Use revenues on the Upper Missouri rate sheet. It corrected that sheet while retaining the conditional-service proposal.

title: Illinois supports a one-time buy, with conditions
speaker: Illinois Commerce Commission
text: The ICC supported a one-time supplemental purchase but wanted protection against forecast error, data for state regulators and no new obligations on states. It warned that a modest percentage error in a larger forecast could mean paying for substantial unneeded capacity.

title: West Virginia prefers to try buyer-seller matching first
speaker: Public Service Commission of West Virginia
text: The commission opposed the original filing in its proposed form and on its proposed timetable. It wanted PJM to learn how much demand would be covered by bilateral contracts before setting a central procurement target.

title: Pennsylvania’s consumer advocate challenges state-set wholesale obligations
speaker: Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate
text: The office argued that PJM was asking states to determine the shares suppliers would owe under a wholesale rate. It asked FERC to reject that design or explain how the new allocation would respect the line between state and federal authority.

title: Who sets a supplier’s share before the bill reaches retail customers?
speaker: Pennsylvania Office of Consumer Advocate
text: Pennsylvania’s consumer advocate objected to relying on states to determine wholesale obligations in the original July proposal. The distinction between a wholesale supplier’s share and retail cost recovery remained relevant when PJM refiled.

title: Data centers ask PJM to recognize self-supply
speaker: Data Center Coalition
text: The coalition supported offsetting a new load’s own capacity purchases and procurement through bilateral deals. It also wanted backstop costs charged to loads driving the need rather than customers elsewhere.

title: Corporate buyers oppose a uniform retail cutoff
speaker: Data Center Coalition
text: The coalition supported letting customers bring their own generation but opposed the proposed interim service. It argued that PJM’s region-wide mandatory curtailment rule would displace state retail decisions.

title: Consumer advocates tie curtailment to an alternative to the backstop
speaker: Joint Consumer Advocates
text: The advocates saw value in a choice between contributing new capacity and curtailing with appropriate state action. With suitable eligibility rules, they argued, this mechanism would make a separate backstop procurement redundant.

title: Mississippi and Arkansas want binding rules filed with FERC
speaker: Mississippi and Arkansas Public Service Commissions
text: The two commissions asked FERC to condition acceptance on putting the specific requirements in the tariff. They said MISO could otherwise change costly requirements through business manuals without comparable review. These are not the same signatories as the LARS comments from Mississippi and Louisiana.

title: Consumer offices challenge the exemption for earlier projects
speaker: Iowa Office of Consumer Advocate, Illinois and Michigan attorneys general, Minnesota Department of Commerce and co-protesters
text: The coalition challenged MISO’s grandfathering provisions. It said existing loads can also trip or ramp suddenly and that utilities and other customers could inherit the cost of local reliability projects if those loads were exempt.
locator: Protest and concluding request on proposed section 37A (unpaginated)

title: State regulators want the export limit to work on the grid as well as on paper
speaker: Organization of MISO States
text: OMS conditionally supported the zero-injection agreement. It wanted enforceable limits on a generator exporting power and asked MISO to explain how paired loads and generators would count in capacity and reliability calculations during outages.

title: West Virginia declined to join the other commissions on the backstop
speaker: Organization of PJM States, recorded member positions
text: OPSI backed a supplemental purchase. Its filing names support from Delaware, D.C., Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and Virginia commissions. The West Virginia commission did not support the comments. OPSI also wanted to recalculate the target when projects withdrew.

title: Kentucky, Ohio and Virginia abstained on the IRAS comments
speaker: Organization of PJM States, recorded member positions
text: Delaware, D.C., Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Tennessee and West Virginia commissions supported OPSI’s comments. Kentucky, Ohio and Virginia commissions abstained. The vote covered the whole filing: OPSI supported a registry but wanted clarification or separate treatment of curtailment compensation.
locator: PDF pp. 1, 7–10, footnote 2 and sections I.D–III

title: States supported the registry while challenging a different payment rule
speaker: Organization of PJM States
text: OPSI supported the registry because states need verified data to allocate retail costs and decide how to curtail load. Its separate objection concerned automatically compensating curtailed projects. Three commissions abstained on the combined comments; that is not a vote against the registry.
locator: PDF pp. 1, 7–10, footnote 2 and sections I.D–III

title: New Jersey wanted one cutoff for counting load across zones
speaker: New Jersey Board of Public Utilities
text: FERC records the board’s comparison of one distributor counting projects from 50 MW and another reporting expansions from 20 MW. The board wanted a consistent threshold so that equally sized projects would not pay differently just because of where they connected.
locator: PDF pp. 43–44, NJBPU comments summarized by FERC

title: New Jersey had objected to uneven starting data
speaker: New Jersey Board of Public Utilities
text: In comments on the July proposal, the board showed how different distributor cutoffs could charge comparable projects differently. It sought a uniform threshold before assigning bills. That objection explains why it matters which projects count in the refiling.
locator: PDF pp. 43–44, NJBPU comments summarized by FERC

title: Ohio’s federal energy advocate favored a state role in retail allocation
speaker: Office of the Federal Energy Advocate, Public Utilities Commission of Ohio
text: FERC records support from the PUCO office for allowing states to determine the allocation to large loads. This is a different office and a different issue from the Ohio Consumers’ Counsel request for confidential registry access.
locator: PDF p. 47, responsive pleadings, citing Ohio FEA comments p. 4

title: Google asked FERC to separate the registry from mandatory interim service
speaker: Google
text: FERC records Google’s request to accept the registry on its own. Google argued that getting better large-load data need not depend on approval of PJM’s wider curtailment and compensation design.
locator: PDF p. 16, ¶36, citing Google protest pp. 3, 18

title: A separate registry was one remedy Google had sought
speaker: Google
text: In the original proceeding Google argued that FERC could accept the registry without accepting the remaining interim-service terms. This predates PJM’s compliance filing implementing that separation.
locator: PDF p. 16, ¶36, citing Google protest pp. 3, 18

title: Google and other buyers ask for state access to cost-allocation data
speaker: Google, Equinix and Data Center Coalition
text: FERC cites all three commenters as seeking to share the underlying allocation data with states. Those data would let a retail regulator see which wholesale obligations had been assigned before setting the customer’s retail rate.
locator: PDF p. 49, footnote 191, citing Google comments p. 8

title: Who pays when a data center brings its own generator?
speaker: Commissioner David LaCerte
text: Answering Senator Cotton, LaCerte said beneficiaries should pay for the new infrastructure and states should hold hyperscalers to their commitments in retail rates. He did not specify a PJM cost formula.
